records.title: Use, cost, and cost trajectories of paid care for people with dementia: longitudinal findings from six years of the IDEAL cohort
records.abstract: This study explores how the service use and paid care costs of people with mild-to-moderate dementia in Britain change over a 7-year period, and which demographic and health characteristics were associated with variations in costs.  We used data collected over six timepoints from the Improving the experience of Dementia and Enhancing Active Life (IDEAL) cohort study and applied regression analysis to estimate costs for sub-groups. Mean marginal effects were estimated to explore paid care cost trajectories following diagnosis.  Hospital and primary care service use remained stable or declined following diagnosis for most of the sample, while care home service use increased. Paid care cost trajectories increased gradually following a diagnosis. Costs varied by dementia sub-type, carer status, depressive symptoms, comorbidities, self-rated health, loneliness, falls, and health-related quality of life.  Dementia sub-type, poor health, loneliness, comorbidities and living alone or being cared for by a non-spousal carer were associated with higher costs. Findings suggest the COVID-19 pandemic strained access to and demand for services.

records.title: Effects of esketamine on postoperative sleep quality in elderly patients under general anesthesia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.abstract: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common disorder among elderly patients undergoing surgery and is associated with a higher risk of adverse outcomes. This meta-analysis investigated the effects of esketamine on postoperative sleep quality among elderly patients.  PubMed, Embase, The Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang databases were searched to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous esketamine with control in elderly patients (≥ 60 years) undergoing elective surgery in general anesthesia. Sleep quality on postoperative day (POD) 1 was the primary outcome. Other outcomes included sleep quality at other time points,  sleep parameters, pain, cognitive function, and adverse events.  Seventeen RCTs involving 2587 patients were included. Regarding the primary outcome, esketamine significantly improved subjective sleep quality on POD 1 (SMD = -0.72; 95% CI, -1.10 to -0.34; I² = 93%), POD 2 (SMD = -1.40; 95% CI, -2.15 to -0.64; I² = 97%), and POD 7 (SMD = -0.38; 95% CI, -0.62 to -0.14; I² = 53%).  sleep measures on POD 1 revealed longer total sleep time, reduced sleep latency, and improved sleep efficiency. Esketamine also decreased pain intensity (SMD = -0.63; 95% CI, -0.88 to -0.38; I² = 70%) and improved MMSE scores (SMD = 0.65; 95% CI, 0.42 to 0.89; I² = 0%). Esketamine was associated with a lower risk of nausea or vomiting. No significant differences was observed between the two groups in terms of dizziness, while hypotension occurred less frequently with esketamine.  Among elderly surgical patients, perioperative esketamine was associated with improved postoperative sleep quality, reduced pain intensity, and a potential improvement in cognitive function, without a significant increase in the risk of major adverse events. However, high-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these findings and determine optimal dosing regimens. Of note, all 17 included trials were conducted in China, potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings to other populations.

records.title: Assessing early-stage acceptability of the adapted version of the lifestyle-integrated functional exercise (aLiFE) programme among community-dwelling Chinese older adults in the UK
records.abstract: Falls are a leading cause of injury and loss of independence among older adults. Although exercise-based interventions can reduce fall risk, sustaining adherence is challenging. The adapted Lifestyle-integrated Functional Exercise (aLiFE) programme addresses this by embedding balance, strength and physical activity tasks into daily routines. However, acceptability depends on whether older adults perceive aLiFE as understandable, manageable, safe and relevant. This may be particularly important for older Chinese adults living in UK, whose language preferences, cultural beliefs, social contexts and health-related experiences may shape perceptions of falls prevention. This study explored initial acceptability and perceived feasibility of aLiFE among older Chinese adults and healthcare professionals in UK.  Community-dwelling older Chinese adults and healthcare partners were purposively recruited in Manchester, UK. Three focus groups with 18 older Chinese adults and three individual interviews with healthcare partners were conducted. Participants completed aLiFE Activity Acceptability Rating Scale and Short Falls Efficacy Scale-International. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, and qualitative data were analysed inductively using Reflexive Thematic Analysis to identify patterns in participants’ views, concerns and recommendations.  Four main themes were identified: (1) Perceived feasibility and practicality of the lifestyle-integrated concept; (2) Usability and accessibility of programme delivery and materials; (3) Perceived burden and accessibility of programme documentation and (4) Acceptability and perceived capability of programme activities. The lifestyle-integrated approach was generally viewed positively as being flexible and compatible with daily routines. Some participants considered documentation burdensome and queried accessibility and credibility of written records. Visual materials and group-based, face-to-face teaching were preferred to written instructions alone. Some activities were viewed as less acceptable because of concerns about safety, confidence and physical discomfort, particularly where tasks involved more challenging balance or strength components. Differences were also observed between older participants and healthcare partners, the latter tending to take a more cautious view of challenging activities and potential risks.  The aLiFE programme was generally perceived as feasible and acceptable among older Chinese adults and healthcare partners. Acceptability depended on how the concept, activities, materials and delivery format were understood and received. These findings provide insights to inform cultural adaptation of aLiFE for this population and support further refinement before wider implementation or evaluation.

records.title: Empty-nest operationalisation and depressive symptoms among rural older Chinese adults: a CHARLS study
records.abstract: Empty-nest status describes household circumstances and is used to identify older adults for administrative attention. We examined how its operationalisation affects classification coverage and the information it provides about concurrent depressive symptoms.  This cross-sectional China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) 2018 analysis included rural adults aged ≥60 years with living children and observed 10-item Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D-10) scores. Proximity-defined empty-nest status required no child living with or nearby the participant; co-residence-defined status required no co-resident child. We compared person-level, household-expanded, and Harmonized CHARLS constructions. Primary association analyses used multiple imputation with community-clustered inference (N = 5,847), with continuous CES-D-10 as the primary outcome and CES-D-10 ≥ 10 as the binary outcome. We assessed fixed-label classification and incremental information beyond a demographic and health benchmark. Complete-case associations were sensitivity analyses; household-composition and 2020 analyses were exploratory.  Among 5,917 eligible participants, proximity status was classifiable for 41.5%, 67.5%, and 98.8% using person-level, household-expanded, and Harmonized constructions, respectively. The primary adjusted mean difference was 0.198 CES-D-10 points (95% confidence interval (CI) − 0.153 to 0.549); the binary-outcome odds ratio was 1.019 (0.897 to 1.158). Direct-label areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) were 0.493 for proximity and 0.495 for co-residence. Adding either label changed apparent AUC by less than 0.001; community-fold cross-validation similarly showed little incremental discrimination. In exploratory analyses, empty-nest participants living alone had higher scores than non-empty-nest participants (mean difference 1.208; 95% CI 0.429 to 1.987), but their direct comparison with empty-nest participants living with other non-spouse members was uncertain (0.858; −0.505 to 2.222).  Among rural older adults with living children in this sample, classification coverage depended on how the empty-nest label was constructed, and the aggregate label conveyed little concurrent symptom information. Studies should report the label definition, construction route, and classification coverage; household status should not substitute for direct symptom information. Exploratory household-group differences warrant longitudinal study; these findings do not validate a screening or referral pathway.

records.title: Stigma moderates the relationship between health literacy and medication adherence among rural elderly pulmonary tuberculosis patients: a cross-sectional study
records.abstract: Rural elderly individuals are a high-risk population for pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB). Medication adherence is critical for treatment success but is often compromised by low health literacy and high stigma. This study aimed to investigate whether stigma moderates the relationship between health literacy and medication adherence.  In December 2024, a consecutive sampling method was used to recruit 283 rural elderly PTB patients who had completed four months of anti-tuberculosis treatment from 18 tuberculosis prevention and control institutions in Henan Province. Sociodemographic and clinical data were collected, and validated Chinese scales for health literacy, stigma, and medication adherence were used. Spearman correlation, simple linear regression, and hierarchical regression (controlling for 9 covariates) were performed to analyze main effects and moderating effects, followed by Johnson‑Neyman analysis and sensitivity analysis.  Health literacy was positively correlated with medication adherence (ρ = 0.227, P P P = 0.010), whereas ordinal logistic regression yielded only marginal significance (OR = 1.004, P = 0.061). Simple slope analysis indicated that the effect of health literacy was not significant at low stigma (b = 0.017, P = 0.303) but was significant and stronger at high stigma (b = 0.076, P 2.72, exceeding which 63.25% of patients fell. Sensitivity analyses showed generally consistent patterns, although the ordinal logistic regression yielded only marginal significance, the moderation finding should therefore be considered exploratory.  The present study offers exploratory evidence suggesting that stigma may play a moderating role in the relationship between health literacy and medication adherence. This moderating pattern suggests that the association between health literacy and adherence may be more pronounced among rural elderly PTB patients with high stigma. Routine assessment of stigma and targeted health education for those with high stigma could be considered, although the efficacy of such stratified strategies remains to be validated by future interventional research. records.title: Staff experiences of person-centred care and quality of life in nursing homes as influenced by leadership and work situation: a qualitative study
records.abstract: PCC is widely recognised as an important approach to supporting QoL in nursing homes. However, staff’s ability to provide PCC may be influenced by leadership and working conditions. There is still limited knowledge of how staff themselves experience performing PCC to support residents’ QoL in everyday nursing home care. The aim of this study was to explore staff experiences of providing PCC to support resident QoL and how their provision of PCC is influenced by leadership and staff working conditions.  A qualitative study design was used. Fifteen semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 enrolled nurses and five nursing assistants working in nursing homes in four Swedish municipalities between February and May 2024. Data were analysed using qualitative conventional content analysis.  An overarching theme, Creating everyday meaning despite challenges , was supported by three categories: Building human relationships in care , Connecting through communication and teamwork , and Overcoming obstacles for person-centred care . Meaningful relationships, attentiveness and tailored support were described as central to providing PCC and supporting residents’ QoL. Communication and teamwork enabled staff to understand and respond to residents’ individual needs, while leadership contributed by supporting staff and facilitating teamwork. Organisational barriers, including staffing shortages, time pressure, communication difficulties and limited leadership support, constrained staff members’ ability to consistently provide PCC and support residents’ QoL.  Staff described a strong intrinsic commitment to providing PCC that supports residents’ QoL. However, their ability to do so was shaped by leadership and organisational conditions. Enabling PCC in nursing homes therefore requires not only staff commitment, but also supportive leadership, adequate staffing and work environments that allow time, communication and continuity in care. records.title: Workplace Ageism, Job Satisfaction, and Depressive Symptoms Among Older Workers: The Roles of US-Born Status
records.abstract: More than 60% of older workers report experiencing ageism in the workplace, yet little is known about whether the relationship between ageism, job satisfaction, and mental health differs by US-born status. This study examined whether job satisfaction mediates the association between workplace ageism and depressive symptoms and assessed whether this association differs by US-born status. Data were drawn from the 2018 and 2020 National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 for workers aged 53- 62, and a multiple-group path analysis was conducted. The  indicated that, among US-born workers, job satisfaction significantly mediated the associations between depressive symptoms and both ageism in promotion and ageism in early retirement. Among immigrant workers, however, this mediating effect was significant only for ageism in promotion. Findings underscore the importance of developing anti-ageism policies that adopt an intersectional approach, jointly considering US-born status and age to reduce the detrimental impacts of ageism on workers’ mental health.

records.title: Intervention-Type-Specific Effects on Healthy Aging of Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
records.abstract: and  Healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment requires preserving physical, cognitive, and psychosocial functioning to sustain their independence and quality of life. However, existing interventions vary in design, delivery format, and composition, and evidence regarding their effectiveness across these three core domains remains inconsistent. This study aimed to identify the most effective intervention types for specific domains of healthy aging. Research Design and  Five electronic databases were searched for studies published from October 2015 to June 2026. Randomized controlled trials reporting at least two outcomes—among physical capability, cognitive function, or psychosocial well-being—were reviewed. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 tool. A dependency-aware multilevel random-effects meta-analysis with trial-clustered robust inference was conducted in R, supplemented by moderator tests, prediction intervals, sensitivity analyses, reporting-bias assessments, and GRADE evaluations.  Multicomponent interventions were associated with beneficial effects on cognitive and psychosocial outcomes, whereas group-based interventions showed beneficial effects across all three domains and a significantly greater effect on cognitive function than individually delivered interventions. Despite substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals, these findings were generally robust across sensitivity analyses.  The observed advantages of group-based delivery, particularly for cognitive function, and multicomponent approaches for cognitive and psychosocial outcomes highlight the domain-specific nature of intervention effects. These findings support tailoring intervention delivery and component configuration to the targeted domain rather than applying a uniform approach to healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment.

records.title: Changes in Instrumental Support Around Retirement: Longitudinal Evidence From Europe
records.abstract: As populations age and the share of retirees increases across Europe, the question of whether individuals stay active after retirement is increasingly salient. Retirees are known to provide more instrumental support than their working counterparts. However, most previous studies have relied on between-group comparisons of retirees and employed individuals, leaving it unclear how the transition into retirement affects changes in instrumental support within individuals over time. Using eight waves of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe covering 19 countries between 2004–2022 (n = 7,422 observations from 3,711 individuals aged 50+), we employed fixed-effects regression and found that the transition from employment to retirement was associated with an increase in instrumental support provision outside the household. We also found suggestive evidence that this association was stronger in countries with higher social expenditures. These findings indicate that retirement may promote activity and facilitate engagement in helping others.

records.title: Impact of Chatbot-Based Cognitive Training on Cognitive Function and White Matter Integrity in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults: Randomized Controlled Trial
records.abstract: Cognitive training may enhance cognition and support brain health during aging, but few trials have evaluated readily accessible chatbot-based programs with neuroimaging outcomes.  This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a chatbot-based cognitive training program on white matter microstructural organization and cognition in cognitively unimpaired older adults.  In a single-blind randomized controlled trial, 72 cognitively unimpaired older adults were assigned to chatbot-based cognitive training (30 min/day, 5 days/week for 12 weeks; n=37) or a no-intervention control (n=35). Diffusion tensor imaging at baseline and 12 weeks quantified fractional anisotropy (FA) in predefined white matter tracts, and cognition was assessed with the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery.  Groups were comparable at baseline. After 12 weeks, the training group showed significantly less FA reduction than controls in the bilateral tapetum and right posterior thalamic radiation, surviving false discovery rate control (P  These findings suggest that a 12-week chatbot-based cognitive training program may support episodic memory and the relative maintenance of white matter microstructural organization in selected pathways in cognitively unimpaired older adults, consistent with a brain-maintenance framework. records.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Digital Exercise-Based Interventions for Improving Balance in Older Adults: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis With GRADE Certainty of Evidence
records.abstract: Technology-based rehabilitation is increasingly used for balance training in older adults. A 2023 network meta-analysis (NMA) found only exergaming with motion capture superior to no treatment; however, the evidence has since expanded, and no GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) appraisal has been applied.  This study aimed to update the comparative effectiveness of 5 technology categories—exergaming with balance platforms (EBP), exergaming with motion capture (EMC), other serious games, interventions with wearables, and telerehabilitation (Tele)—versus conventional exercise (CE), and no treatment (NT), applying GRADE adapted for NMA.  A systematic search of 4 databases from inception through April 2025, with an identical supplementary update search to January 31, 2026, identified 60 randomized controlled trials (N=3469; mean age 73.1, SD 5.2; range 63.3-86.2 y). Fifty-seven trials (2758 analyzed participants) contributed to 4 prespecified networks (all balance, functional scales, Timed Up and Go [TUG] test, and gait speed). A random-effects NMA was fitted using multivariate meta-regression. Treatment hierarchies were summarized by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) and the probability of being best; certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE adapted for NMA.  In the all-balance network, Tele (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.69, 95% CI 0.08‐1.29; P =.03), EBP (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.31‐0.95; P P =.002), and CE (SMD 0.35, 95% CI 0.03‐0.68; P =.03) were superior to NT, with consistent findings in the TUG network (EBP 0.81, 95% CI 0.42‐1.20; Tele 0.82, 95% CI 0.16‐1.49; EMC 0.79, 95% CI 0.36‐1.21; all P P =.41).  Tele, EBP, and EMC were each associated with improved balance versus NT, although none exceeded CE. The first-place SUCRA ranking of Tele is preliminary. Certainty was moderate only for EBP and EMC versus NT on the TUG test; the remaining evidence is too uncertain for firm clinical recommendations. As no included trial reported falls, these findings are not direct evidence of fall prevention. Larger trials with standardized comparator intensity and posttraining follow-up are required.

records.title: Orthostatic blood pressure fluctuations and risk of falls in community-dwelling older adults: the role of recovery time
records.abstract: Available literature related to the association between orthostatic blood pressure (BP) variations and falls is controversial. We analyzed how orthostatic hypo- (OH) and hypertension (OHTN) relate to falls considering recovery time (RT) in community-dwelling older adults.  This analysis uses data from the ActiFE cohort. BP was measured lying, immediately, 1, 2 and 3 min after standing. Systolic OH (sOH) and systolic OHTN (sOHTN) indicate a systolic BP (SBP) drop or increment ≥20 mm Hg, respectively. OH and OHTN further consider a diastolic BP (DBP) drop or increment ≥10 mm Hg. RT was categorized as Early Recovery (  Among 509 subjects (mean age 79 years, 44% female, 168 falls), prevalences were: 16.5% sOH, 26.9% OH, 9.0% sOHTN and 15.5% OHTN. Overall, OH was not associated with falls. However, falls risk increased with Delayed (OR 3.11 [95% CI 1.21-8.01]) and NoRecovery (OR 4.04 [95% CI 1.07-15.26]). sOH showed an adjusted OR of 2.00 [95% CI 1.15-3.47] for at least one fall. Regarding RT the risk of falls was increased in Delayed (OR 4.73 [95% CI 1.71-13.10]) and No Recovery (OR 5.06 [95% CI 1.42-22.27]). OHTN was not associated with falls.  Overall, only sOH was associated with falls. When RT was considered, those with Delayed and No Recovery showed higher risk of falls regardless of the OH definition used.

records.title: Detection of Age-Related Cognitive Decline Over Short Time Frames Using Digital Multiday Learning Assessments: Longitudinal Study
records.abstract: High-resolution digital cognitive tools administered at frequent intervals enable the study of age-related cognitive change at a previously unattainable level of granularity. The  of this study was to examine whether repeated digital multiday learning assessments can detect age-related cognitive decline over short time frames in cognitively unimpaired older adults and to quantify age-related differences in process-based cognitive markers derived from computational modeling.  A total of 209 cognitively unimpaired older adults (mean age 73.6, SD 8.2 years; n=136, 65.1% female) from the Harvard Aging Brain Study and affiliated studies were administered the Boston Remote Assessment for Neurocognitive Health, which includes the face-name task, a paired associative learning task. Daily median response times for correct responses were used as the primary outcome. A new version of the face-name task was administered across up to 4 testing intervals over a mean of 2.8 (SD 0.4) years. Using computational modeling, we estimated longitudinal changes in peak performance, a practice-adjusted marker of an individual’s best expected response time, as an indicator of age-related cognitive decline. records.title: A Longitudinal Study on Social Isolation, Chronic Diseases, and Depressive Symptoms: Evidence From the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging
records.abstract: This study examined the longitudinal effects of social isolation on chronic diseases and depressive symptoms among middle-aged and older adults in South Korea, with attention to gender and age differences. Method Using data from three waves of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging, longitudinal path analysis was conducted on 5,585 participants.  Women and older adults showed higher levels of social isolation, chronic diseases, and depressive symptoms, indicating greater vulnerability. Significant longitudinal and bidirectional associations emerged among social isolation, chronic diseases, and depressive symptoms over time. While gender differences in long-term patterns were modest, age-related disparities were more substantial.  These findings underscore the importance of strengthening community-based social networks and implementing both conventional outreach—such as home visits—and innovative approaches, including technology-assisted companionship, to identify socially isolated individuals, particularly older adults.

records.title: Need-Conditioned Uncertainty and Perceived Non-Provision of Community Services: Social Participation and Functional Status Among Older Adults in Urban China
records.abstract: Older adults who need community services may remain uncertain whether those services are locally provided or judge that they are not. Research on perceived unmet need often combines these positions. Using a cross-sectional survey of 929 adults aged 60 or older in urban Jiangsu, China, we paired reported need with perceived provision across 20 services and distinguished awareness gaps, perceived non-provision, and comparison uncertainty for services not reported as needed. Fractional logit models examined associations with social participation and functional status. Greater social participation was associated with fewer awareness gaps, concentrated among adults with ADL disability (−8.75 percentage points per SD). A weaker, less stable association with perceived non-provision appeared among functionally independent adults, and no counterpart appeared for comparison uncertainty. Unresolved uncertainty and negative provision judgments may call for different responses, and outreach may be especially relevant for older adults with ADL disability.

records.title: Delirium Occurrence and Associated Factors Among Patients With Dementia and Mild Cognitive Impairment Admitted to Long-Term Care Hospitals: Cross-Sectional Study
records.abstract: Delirium is common among older adults, particularly those with cognitive impairment. However, delirium among patients with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in long-term care (LTC) hospitals has received limited attention.  This study aimed to examine delirium occurrence and associated factors among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals.  This cross-sectional study included 142 patients aged 65 years or older with dementia (n=100, 70.4%) or MCI (n=42, 29.6%) at 2 LTC hospitals in South Korea between September 2021 and August 2022. Delirium occurrence was defined as at least 1 positive Short Confusion Assessment Method assessment during twice-daily assessments over 4 weeks, including the first assessment. Multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors overall and within each cognitive group.  Delirium was identified in 55 (38.7%) of 142 patients. The proportion was 41% (41/100) in patients with dementia and 33.3% (14/42) in patients with MCI. Hypoactive delirium was the most common subtype (33/55, 60%). Overall, female sex (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 4.344, 95% CI 1.794-10.515; P=.001), immobility (aOR 4.953, 95% CI 1.857-13.205; P=.001), and analgesic use (aOR 3.641, 95% CI 1.262-10.501; P=.02) were associated with delirium. Infection was inversely associated with delirium (aOR 0.251, 95% CI 0.101-0.623; P=.003). In patients with dementia, female sex, immobility, analgesic use, and pain were associated with delirium. Diaper use was associated with delirium in patients with MCI.  Delirium was common among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals. The findings support regular delirium assessment, with attention to mobility and pain-related care needs. Further studies are needed to clarify the factors associated with delirium in each cognitive group.

records.title: Does incident multimorbidity mediate the relationship between lifetime trauma and trajectories of cognitive function in later life?
records.abstract: and  Prior research has examined the relationship between traumatic experiences and cognitive function in adulthood. We build on this literature by using a life course perspective to ask whether incident multimorbidity mediates the relationship between lifetime trauma and trajectories of cognitive function. Research Design and  We use latent growth curve models and data from the 2010-2020 waves of the Health and Retirement Study (N = 16,662) to examine the relationship between lifetime trauma, incident multimorbidity, and the intercept and slope of cognitive function.   indicate that trauma is associated with a higher intercept of cognitive function and greater cognitive decline. Lifetime trauma is also associated with higher risk of incident multimorbidity, which, in turn, is associated with a lower intercept of cognitive function.  Incident multimorbidity has an upstream influence on poor cognitive function among people exposed to trauma. Interventions may be needed for people exposed to trauma over the life course to reduce the risk of disease and cognitive decline in later life.

records.title: Yearning to Be Our Younger Self: The Relationship Between Grief and Yearning to Internalized Ageism and Ableism
records.abstract: Internalized ageist and ableist beliefs significantly influence health outcomes, happiness, and longevity. Idealization of youth and pervasive ageist and ableist narratives devalue aging, contributing to perceptions of later life and potentially fostering grief over lost opportunities. To develop evidence-based interventions, it is essential to examine the potential relationship between grief, yearning, and fears about aging. A cross-sectional survey was conducted using ResearchMatch, and 384 individuals responded to questions regarding ageism, ableism, and experiences with grief. Yearning was significantly associated with internalized ageism, excessive fear of aging, and loss of physical health. Grief was significantly associated with age, internalized ageism, and excessive fear of aging. Interventions to address feelings of loss as we age, both experienced and anticipated, can be developed to address and improve personal attitudes toward growing older.

records.title: Mental Health Burden and Vulnerability Among Long-Term Care Facility Residents During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Systematic Review With Exploratory Prevalence Meta-Analysis
records.abstract: Older adults in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) faced social and care disruptions during COVID-19, but evidence on mental health burden and vulnerability remains fragmented.  To synthesise evidence on mental health outcomes among LTCF residents during the pandemic and identify resident- and facility-level vulnerability and protective conditions.  MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO were searched for English-language peer-reviewed studies published from January 2020 to January 2025. Findings were narratively synthesised, and exploratory random-effects meta-analyses were conducted where at least three studies reported extractable resident-level prevalence.  Thirty-two studies were included as follows: 24 quantitative, six qualitative and two mixed-. Most reported high prevalence, deterioration, or qualitative evidence of depression, anxiety, loneliness, isolation, or related distress. Pooled prevalence was 55.6% for depression, 51.4% for anxiety and 54.5% for loneliness, with substantial heterogeneity. Vulnerability reflected clinical, social and facility-level factors; consistent staffing, social connection and family communication were potential protective conditions.

records.title: Feasibility of a Co-Designed Personalized Cognitive Reablement Program Delivered via Digital Voice Assistants for Older Adults Living With Early-Stage Dementia or Mild Cognitive Impairment: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
records.abstract: Home-based reablement programs have improved everyday functioning for people living with early-stage dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but the substantial time commitment required for delivery by health professionals has created a barrier to widespread implementation. Digital technology could facilitate delivery, but traditional devices such as smartphones and tablets present usability challenges for this population. We have co-designed a cognitive reablement program, VOICE-COG, that can deliver personalized interventions broadcast via voice-controlled digital voice assistants (DVAs).  This pilot nonblinded randomized controlled trial examined the feasibility and potential effectiveness of VOICE-COG for older adults living with dementia or MCI to guide the design of a full-scale trial.  Older adults (aged 60‐85 years) with a self-reported diagnosis of dementia or MCI (N=30) were recruited via Facebook or the StepUp-for Dementia Research database and randomized to either a DVA intervention (n=15) or control (n=15) group for 12 weeks. Each participant randomized to the intervention group and their care partner met with a psychologist via Zoom to select 2 or 3 personalized goals from the VOICE-COG program. The personalized program was input into the software (BuddyLink) by researchers for broadcast via a DVA (Amazon Alexa Show 8). Participants in the control group received enhanced usual care, consisting of treatment as usual, plus weekly informational emails. Primary feasibility outcomes were recruitment, retention, device-recorded adherence, and the System Usability Scale (SUS). Secondary outcomes were self-reported by the participant and care partner via web-based Qualtrics forms and included the Goal Attainment Scale–Light (GAS), changes in participant mood, cognition, and everyday functioning, and carer burden.  The recruitment rate was 86% (30/35) and the retention rate was 97% (29/30), with 1 participant in the intervention group lost to follow-up. Adherence to the VOICE-COG program ranged from 29% to 100% (mean 70%, SD 17%). The VOICE-COG program was rated as marginally acceptable (mean SUS score 56.3, SD 18.1). After 12 weeks, 60% (9/15) of the intervention group reported having met or exceeded their goals (GAS-Light t-score ≥50; mean 57.6, SD 15.4). The intervention group had a significantly higher increase in Multifactorial Memory Questionnaire–Strategy subscale score compared with control, mean difference 5.0 (95% CI 0.03-10.1, P =.049), representing a medium effect size ( d =0.55). There were no other significant differences between groups.  This co-designed VOICE-COG program, delivered via DVAs, was feasible for older adults living with early-stage dementia or MCI, resulting in most participants meeting their reablement goals and increases in the use of memory strategies. System usability issues should be addressed in future adequately powered trials.

records.title: The Prevalence of Dementia Diagnosis and Delivery of Appropriate Dementia Care in Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services
records.abstract: This study aimed to assess the recorded prevalence of a dementia diagnosis and the receipt of appropriate dementia care among current Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clients of Aboriginal and Community Controlled Health Services (ACCHS) aged 45 and over, as documented in medical records. ACCHSs are Australian primary healthcare organisations that are initiated, governed and operated by local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. A manual audit of medical records was undertaken by a staff member from each participating ACCHS to identify current clients with a documented diagnosis of dementia and examine their receipt of key elements of dementia-related care. Across 9 ACCHSs located in New South Wales, a total of 70 clients with a recorded diagnosis of dementia were identified (1.2% recorded prevalence rate). The majority of clients with a dementia diagnosis had documented receipt of elements of appropriate dementia care including an active chronic disease management plan (61%), annual health assessment (56%), referral to aged care services (69%), and assessment of one or more dementia-related risks (94%). However, less than half of clients had a documented cognitive assessment within the last 12 months (41%) or completed any advance planning documentation (37%). Clients with a dementia diagnosis received a mean of 3.6 out of 6 assessed elements of best practice dementia care. As with primary care nationally and internationally, ACCHSs require co-designed support strategies to enhance their processes for dementia diagnosis and documentation and to build upon their delivery of best-practice dementia care. Priority dementia care areas for older clients with a confirmed dementia diagnosis include the evaluation of dementia-related risks such as elder abuse and driving safety, and the implementation of advance care planning including discussion or completion of relevant legal documents. records.title: What do young adults think about informal care for older adults?: Testing and validation of a public caregiver stigma scale in Canada
records.abstract: and  Young adults are the caregivers of tomorrow. However, it remains unclear what stereotypes about informal caregiving for older adults they have learned. This study aimed to test and validate a first of its kind scale to measure public caregiver stigma as perceived among young adults without prior care experiences. Research Design and  Participants aged 18 to 35 years, collected from the community (sample 1) and university students (sample 2) in Canada answered a self-reported online survey on public caregiver stigma (Public Caregiver Stigma Scale, Warmth-Competence-Scale) and their sociodemographic . Exploratory (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor analyses (CFA) were conducted, and the resulting scale was tested for content and concurrent validity and reliability.  : The EFA performed on sample 1 resulted in a two-factor model with correlated factors that was confirmed by a CFA in sample 2, demonstrating excellent model fit. Content and concurrent validity were supported by the study’s findings and internal consistency of the two scales varied between acceptable and good. Young adults showed moderately high positive and negative public caregiver stigma, which were associated with their sociodemographic characteristics.  The study confirmed a new quantitative measure of public caregiver stigma targeting unpaid caregiving for older adults, reflecting negative (e.g., isolation, invisibility) and positive (e.g., admiration) stereotypes, emotional, and behavioral reactions. records.title: Global Frameworks Toward Effective Integration of Technology in National Dementia Strategies: Narrative Review and Case Study in Mexico
records.abstract: Population aging is a global phenomenon that has led to a rise in age-related conditions, particularly dementia. This situation presents significant challenges for health care systems, caregivers, and society as a whole. Technologies have shown potential to address the needs of people living with dementia and their caregivers, offering support in daily activities, communication, and care monitoring. However, only a quarter of countries worldwide have developed national dementia plans, and even fewer have integrated technology-based solutions into these policies.  This study aimed to analyze existing gaps in dementia plans, with a particular emphasis on the limited integration of technological solutions as essential tools for dementia care and management. Based on this analysis, this study proposes a framework to facilitate context-appropriate technology integration.  This study presents a narrative review of public policy frameworks for dementia care. The review provides a global overview, examines the context in Latin America, and focuses on Mexico as a case study to analyze how technology is integrated into dementia strategies.  Based on these findings, this study proposes a framework of general recommendations adaptable across multiple countries. Furthermore, it demonstrates the application of this framework in Mexico to strengthen its national dementia strategy through technological solutions tailored to people living with dementia and their informal caregivers.  Given that dementia is recognized as a global priority, countries with aging populations have developed numerous technological solutions. These international experiences serve as valuable references to guide the adoption or rejection of specific approaches, provided that local cultural and social contexts are considered. The applied technologies were merged into a framework that can be adapted to different countries, taking into account social aspects, governance, and region-specific barriers to generate a viable, customized option, as demonstrated in the case study focused on Mexico.

records.title: Greenspace Exposure During Everyday Mobility and Working Memory in Older Adults: Momentary Benefits Amid Stressors
records.abstract: Introduction. While residential greenspace has been linked to better cognitive function in older adults, it remains unclear whether short-term greenspace exposure during everyday mobility can provide immediate cognitive benefits. Stress may play a critical role in this process, as it reflects a mismatch between environmental demands and personal resources and may signal an increased need for restoration. . This ambulatory assessment study examined the association between greenspace exposure and cognition in daily life, as well as the moderating role of stress. Over a two-week period, 123 older adults (aged 65–89 years) wore a GPS device that continuously recorded their mobility trajectories and carried a smartphone to complete repeated working memory tasks and experience sampling assessments of stressors approximately every two hours (seven times per day). . Multilevel models showed that, at the within-person level, greater-than-usual greenspace exposure in the past two hours was associated with higher-than-usual momentary working memory performance when stressor occurrence was reported, compared to moments when stressors were not reported. At the between-person level, individuals with higher overall greenspace exposure showed better working memory performance. . These findings suggest that the cognitive benefits of greenspace exposure are context-dependent, emerging when stressors were recently present and when the need for restoration may be high. More broadly, our findings point to a dynamic, needs-based process in which everyday mobility through natural environments may support cognitive health among older adults.

records.title: Network Analysis of Depressive Symptoms Among Chinese Older Adults Across Different Intergenerational Support Patterns
records.abstract: Intergenerational support plays a crucial role in mental health in later life, yet both the heterogeneity of support patterns and the symptom-level interplay among depressive symptoms remain underexplored. Network analysis and the Network Comparison Test (NCT) were utilized to estimate and compare depressive symptom networks (CESD-10) across subgroups.  Three patterns emerged: Distant-Supportive (55.9%), Proximate-Interactive (24.2%), and Traditional Co-resident (19.9%). While “sadness” and “being bothered” were universal core symptoms, NCT revealed distinct structural disparities. The Proximate-Interactive group exhibited a uniquely strong “bothered–fearful” connection. The Distant-Supportive group showed pronounced “effort–cannot get going” pathways, whereas the Traditional Co-resident group displayed a stronger “bothered–trouble focusing” link.  Intergenerational support patterns are not only associated with overall depression severity but also with differences in the network topology of depressive symptoms. Differentiated interventions tailored to specific family structures are essential for geriatric mental health.

records.title: Age trajectories of informal caregiving for older people in England: Testing the healthy caregiver hypothesis
records.abstract: and  This study investigates how health status shapes the age trajectories of informal caregiving for spouses and older parents in England. Research Design and  The data came from five waves (2012–2023) of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). We analysed 41,997 person-wave observations from 12,420 individuals aged 50+. We derived a latent health construct via hierarchical confirmatory factor analysis, integrating functional, mental, physical, and cognitive domains. Dynamic random-effects models were employed to examine the influence of prior health on consequent caregiving, and initial condition adjustment was made to correct estimation bias.  Among those with a spouse, parents, or parents-in-law, healthier individuals demonstrated steeper increases in caregiving probability over time, while those in poor health showed flatter or declining caregiving trajectories. For spousal caregiving, better health was associated with a lower likelihood of caregiving at age 50, but this relationship turned positive from age 70 onwards. For parental caregiving, better health was associated with a higher likelihood of caregiving from age 53 onwards.  Overall the research findings are consistent with the healthy caregiver hypothesis, particularly in later life. Good health facilitates the provision of informal care, whereas poor health compromises caregiving capability and constitutes a barrier to taking on a caregiving role. records.title: Balance on the Brain: Multimodal exercise programme evaluating physical performance, falls, quality of life and cognition for people with mild cognitive impairment-randomised controlled trial
records.abstract: and  The aim of this study was to evaluate whether a balance-focused multimodal exercise programme improves balance and reduces falls for people with mild cognitive impairment. Research Design and  A single-blind randomised controlled trial (n = 128, before withdrawals), with 6-month intervention, followed by 6-month maintenance period. The intervention, Balance on the Brain, consisted of three exercise programmes: walking, Balance Yourself and Clock Yourself.  Data from 126 adults with mild cognitive impairment were included in the study (median age = 76, 63% female). The study did not meet the required sample size to be fully powered for either falls or balance primary outcomes. Therefore, the lack of significant between-group differences for the primary outcomes of falls or balance at 6 and 12-months remains inconclusive, due to insufficient power. Fifty-nine percent (n = 38) of intervention participants were identified as adherers. Adherers’ balance improved significantly compared to low-adherers/controls at 6 and 12-months and intervention adherers fell less than low-adherers/controls, although the difference was not significant. However, the adherers data were exploratory and need to be used with caution.  Balance on the Brain was underpowered and as such the non-significant primary balance and falls outcomes should be interpreted as inconclusive for people living with mild cognitive impairment in the community. Those who adhered demonstrated improved balance, and reduced falls compared to low-adherers/controls, however these data should be interpreted as exploratory and with caution.

records.title: Spending time helping others and well-being of givers: Age differences in immediate and long-term effects on well-being
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: The extant literature suggests that spending time helping others is associated with both beneficial and detrimental effects on givers’ emotional experiences. To reconcile these findings, the current study examined the daily- and monthly-level associations between spending time helping others and well-being. We predicted that spending time helping others would be associated with lower hedonic well-being at the daily level but higher eudaimonic well-being at the monthly level. We further hypothesized that age would moderate these associations. Method We used data from the main survey and the National Study of Daily Experiences (NSDE) in MIDUS 3 (N=865) and MIDUS Refresher 1 (N=612). Participants reported their daily and monthly time spent helping others. Measures included hedonic well-being (negative affect and positive affect) and eudaimonic well-being (social and psychological well-being).  At the daily level, our sample of adults experienced mixed emotional consequences on days when they spent more time helping others, reporting both higher negative and positive affect. Age moderation showed young and middle-aged adults experienced more negative affect. At the monthly level, spending time helping others was associated with higher social and psychological well-being. This association was significantly stronger among older adults than middle-aged adults in Refresher 1. Monthly spending time helping others was not associated with hedonic well-being. Discussion These findings suggest that spending time helping others can be both taxing and enjoyable in the short term while contributing to eudaimonic benefits over the long term. Older age may reduce costs and enhance benefits of spending time helping others.

records.title: Emergent Connections: A Community-Based Model for Advancing Social Connection Among Immigrant Older Adults with Disabilities
records.abstract: and  Social isolation is an urgent public health concern, especially for older immigrants who face heightened barriers to social participation due to disability, structural health inequities, and limited access to culturally and linguistically appropriate services. This study presents a programmatic model that explains how social connection and sustained participation can be fostered through accessible, culturally responsive, and participatory design. Research Design and  This community-engaged case study examines a national virtual program serving Spanish-speaking older adults, many of whom have sensory disabilities and chronic illnesses. A thematic and comparative analysis was conducted using qualitative interviews with ten older adults with vision impairment, program documents, and consultation with program leadership. This led to the identification of a programmatic model, the emergent connections platform.  The emergent connections platform strengthens loosely connected social networks among older adults who share cultural and lived experiences through three pillars. The first is cultural, linguistic, and physically accessible infrastructure. Second, shared governance cultivates member leadership and program co-creation. Third, a flexible structure allows for evolution in response to member needs and innovations. These pillars collectively create pathways for individuals to engage, lead, and strengthen their communities.  Advancing a more inclusive democracy requires sustained investment in accessible, community-led initiatives that support the leadership and innovation of marginalized older adults. This calls for moving towards models that position older adults as co-creators of programs and services. Doing so cultivates social connection through leadership, reciprocity, and a sense of belonging within a broader social fabric.

records.title: Determinants of Self-Care Practices Among Family Caregivers of Older Adults with Chronic Illness: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
records.abstract: and  Caregiver burden significantly impedes self-care, often resulting in poor health and increased vulnerability to chronic illness. Despite these risks, the underlying factors influencing caregivers’ self-care remain understudied. This qualitative descriptive study explored the context of caregiver self-care and identified perceived barriers and facilitators to practicing self-care. Research Design and  We conducted four focus groups with 14 caregivers primarily responsible for providing in-home care to older adults (≥ 65 years) with chronic illnesses. Focus groups were audio-recorded and transcribed. A hierarchical coding system was developed and refined using the focus group guide and preliminary transcript review. Coded transcripts were analyzed using an iterative inductive-deductive thematic approach based on established theories.  Caregivers’ multi-dimensional definitions of self-care shaped their perceived barriers and facilitators. Three core determinants of self-care behaviors were identified: capability (caregivers’ psychological and physical health, and behavioral regulation); motivation (caregiver identity, emotions, and perceived control); and opportunity (social and environmental influences and resources). Caregivers recognized that self-care deficits negatively affect their clinical, behavioral, and psychosocial outcomes. These  informed the development of a conceptual framework for caregiver self-care.  Findings underscore the importance of integrating caregivers’ own perceptions of self-care into support models. Interventions should transition toward personalized approaches that address both intrinsic psychological drivers and extrinsic environmental constraints. The framework derived from this study provides a theory-driven roadmap that informs future interventions, ensuring support systems align with caregivers’ unique needs and contexts to foster better self-care and ultimately enhance their health outcomes.

records.title: Drafting the next chapter: A scoping review of academic retirement planning
records.abstract: and  Interest in retirement planning among university faculty has grown in recent years as more academics approach traditional retirement age. This scoping review examines the current literature on retirement planning among higher education faculty by examining study characteristics; participant characteristics; theoretical frameworks employed; factors influencing retirement planning; and the quality of the included studies. Research Design and  A comprehensive search across Medline, Embase, APA PsycInfo, AgeLine, ERIC, Education Source, Business Source Premier, Sociological Abstracts, International Bibliography of the Social Sciences, JSTOR, and Web of Science Core Collection yielded an initial dataset of 8,906 unique articles. Following full-text assessment, 44 studies met the inclusion criteria.  Five factors prevailed across this literature as key mechanisms in academic retirement planning, including: 1) financial security; 2) health factors; 3) age and/or institutional policies; 4) work, family, and lifestyle factors; and 5) professional identity. Participant characteristics such as age, gender, stage of retirement, and other characteristics of the academic environment were reported inconsistently across the literature; only 14 of the studies mentioned a theoretical framework.  This is the first scoping review of academic retirement with a focus on planning that includes a range of . While health and financial security remain central to retirement planning broadly, the studies in this review suggest that professional identity plays a distinct role in shaping how academics approach retirement planning. Implications include the need for longitudinal designs to capture how faculty transitions, shifting professional identities, and planning behaviors evolve dynamically over time.
